newsitem.title: South Africa: South Africa to host first Zairean peace talks.
newsitem.headline: South Africa to host first Zairean peace talks.

text.p: Representatives of the warring parties in Zaire plan to meet for the first time in Cape Town on Thursday, South African President Nelson Mandela said.

Mandela said after a five-nation summit on Wednesday to discuss crises in sub-Saharan Africa that the initiative had come jointly from the government of Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko and from Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
"Representatives of the contesting parties have made a request that they would like to meet in South Africa...to be able to discuss their problems," Mandela said.
"If arrangements go according to plan, these parties should be here tomorrow. The request is that they want to meet here themselves. We will not interfere unless they ask us to do so."
Neither the Zairean government nor the rebels fighting in the east have confirmed their participation.
Mandela lauded Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni for facilitating the initiative, saying:

"President Museveni has started what we believe is a very good initiative where he is appealing to the parties to declare a truce, a ceasefire, and also to set up a structure to prepare for elections in Zaire.
"I think they are coming here because they want to respond to this initiative," he said.

Museveni and presidents Quett Masire of Botswana, Robert Mugabe of Zimbabwe and Joaquim Chissano of Mozambique joined Mandela for the summit which looked also at problems in Lesotho, Swaziland and Angola.
Mandela said proposals agreed would not be made public until all leaders of the 12-nation Southern African Development Community had been briefed.
Fighting in Zaire has intensified, with the ailing Mobutu's government launching air strikes this week on rebels who have seized much of the east of the country since October.
Zaire says rebels are backed by troops from neighbouring Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi, which deny any involvement.
Zaire has sent mixed signals on peace talks, with senior figures repeatedly calling for a military solution. In the past, it has ruled out talks while foreign troops remain on its soil.
South African officials had said Mandela, seen by many Africans as their continent's greatest hope for peace, sought a political response to the problem.
"The idea of military intervention is very much on the back burner," one said.

A diplomatic source in Cape Town said a special envoy of Mobutu visited South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki on Sunday and put proposals to him for discussion at a meeting on Monday between Mbeki and U.S. Vice President Al Gore.
The source said the two men contacted Kabila and persuaded him to agree to a meeting in South Africa, where it was believed confidentiality and security could be guaranteed.
Mobutu's envoy had remained "in the region", the source said, adding that the approach had been welcomed as one in line with Mandela's drive for an African dispute-resolution plan.
South African officials declined to say what role Mandela or his government might play in the meeting, which could be the first breakthrough in a slide towards civil war in Zaire.
"All we're doing is facilitating a very important meeting between the two contending parties," one official said.
